items.title: Nation’s largest grocery chain cuts thousands of jobs — sparks fury over who it’s hiring instead: 'Insanity'
items.summary:
Kroger, the largest traditional grocery chain in the nation, is facing strong blowback on social media over its plan to slash 3,000 jobs in the United States while advertising new positions overseas in India.

The controversy comes as the Cincinnati-based grocer begins executing a three-year plan it has previously announced to cut $5 billion in costs as part of a restructuring that will eliminate roughly 37% of its U.S. corporate workforce by 2029.

While Kroger maintains the reductions are aimed at lowering shelf prices through technology and leaner operations, simultaneous recruiting for a new hub in Bangalore has fueled online accusations that the company is offshoring American jobs while asking shoppers to bear high food prices.

"‘They’re doing the jobs Americans don’t want to do, ’" Theo Wold, a former White House deputy assistant for domestic policy during President Donald Trump's first term, posted on X. "No. They are taking jobs from Americans because it’s cheaper for corporations to hire foreigners."
items.t: Nation’s largest grocery chain cuts thousands of jobs — sparks fury over who it’s hiring instead: 'Insanity'

items.title: Senate GOP takes risky bet on Dems as holiday shutdown deadline looms: 'It's a gamble'
items.summary:
Congress is nearing the deadline to avert a government shutdown, and Senate Republicans are taking a leap of faith as the clock ticks: trusting Senate Democrats to dodge a holiday disaster.

When the upper chamber returns on Nov. 30, there will be just shy of two weeks for both sides to reach an agreement to thwart another partisan closure. At the center of the issue is the Iran war: Democrats intend to use the government’s purse strings to bring the eight-month conflict to an end.

Republicans, meanwhile, want to put together an emergency supplemental funding package with hundreds of billions of dollars dedicated to the military, munitions and war effort. They have, for now, pressed pause on ramming those tax dollars through the party-line budget reconciliation process, and instead are opening the door to work with Democrats.

DEMOCRATS COULD ENTER CONGRESSIONAL MAJORITY IN A GOVERNMENT SHUTDOWN

There’s history here: Senate Democrats have twice now ushered in a government shutdown. And though Republicans agreed behind closed doors to move forward with their counterparts, they know it’s a leap in the dark.

"Each side is a gamble," Sen. Tim Sheehy, R-Mont., told Fox News Digital.

"I mean, obviously, if it's partyline, when you look at the House side, you know, we got…
items.t: Senate GOP takes risky bet on Dems as holiday shutdown deadline looms: 'It's a gamble'

"To any red-blooded patriot or business wanting to flee the woke-show that is coming to Texas… Alabama is open for business," Tuberville, a Republican, wrote Monday on X.

Tuberville was responding to a video shared by Libs of TikTok, an account run by a conservative influencer, that appears to show an event hosted by Equality Texas, a pro-LGBTQ+ advocacy group.

DAN PATRICK CONCEDES TEXAS 'TURNED PURPLE' AFTER DEMOCRATS' HISTORIC BLUE WAVE

"Texas is Black. Texas is gay. Texas is trans. Texas is indigenous. Texas is lesbian. Texas is all of us," the speaker is heard saying in the clip.

This comes after Democrats swept statewide races in Texas and flipped the governor’s office, a U.S. Senate seat and the Texas House, while Republicans managed to maintain control of the Texas Senate.

items.title: What do Brexit and an Australian cricket scandal have in common? Sometimes it’s right to reopen old wounds | Jonathan Liew
items.summary:
Just like the ball-tampering scandal of 2018, the Brexit debate is back. The lesson here is that anything with a dodgy whiff about it will only come back

Just move on. You lost, get on with it. Why rake up the past? And why, for the love of all that is holy, is Theresa May back on my television?

Of all the many regrettable political figures to have surfaced over recent days, perhaps May has been most triggering of all: a bleak reminder of unhappier times. But of course she has been far from the only former prime minister lured from obscurity by the irresistible siren call of Brexit Revisited. David Cameron has been portending a “very long and painful argument”. “Divisive” and “all-consuming”, argued Rishi Sunak. Boris Johnson warned Andy Burnham – with no apparent sense of irony – that reopening the Brexit negotiations would be “wasting his premiership”. Here they come, the cast of the Tory remake of Avengers: Doomsday, presaging of rancour and paralysis from the people who brought us years of rancour and paralysis.

Jonathan Liew is a sportswriter and Opinion columnist for the Guardian

Continue reading...
items.t: What do Brexit and an Australian cricket scandal have in common? Sometimes it’s right to reopen old wounds | Jonathan Liew

items.title: The Guardian view on disability benefits: Timms’s radical review is rooted in experience | Editorial
items.summary:
Ministers have taken on board their MPs’ message about cuts. Now anxious claimants need reassurance

Four million people with disabilities or long‑term health conditions in the UK claim personal independence payment (Pip). A review by Sir Stephen Timms, the social security minister, offers a blueprint for how to overhaul it. Its recommendations pose a difficult question for ministers: are they prepared to meet the needs that a more accurate assessment of the costs of disability might reveal?

Sir Stephen worked as one of three co-chairs with a steering group of 12 people with a range of professional and lived experience. There is broad agreement that Pip needs to be reformed. The announcement on Tuesday that the government would accept the recommendation of a new fast track for claimants whose conditions are lifelong or unlikely to improve, and abolish unnecessary benefit reviews, signalled that ministers are ready for change. The decision, affecting one in 10 claimants in England and Wales, is welcome but long overdue. Ministers should work with the devolved administrations to ensure similar progress elsewhere in the UK.

His predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, had notoriously warned ministers against being “overly deferential” in discussions with the devolved administrations. But Mr Burnham’s signature commitment to distributing more power and responsibility out of Westminster, and his consensual style, appeared to augur well for a positive reset in relations.

In Wales, this early optimism has just been brutally quashed by an uncharacteristically peremptory letter from Mr Burnham to the first minister, Rhun ap Iorwerth. items.title: Farage preaches the Brexit gospel according to St Nige | John Crace
items.summary:
Reform leader is happy to return to his anti-EU happy place, where the truth can be whatever you want it to be

This feels like Nigel Farage’s happy place. It’s hardly a secret that he prefers his own company. His fellow Reform MPs are a necessary inconvenience at best. Muppets at worst. He can barely hide his misogyny for Sarah Pochin, having written her off as a pisshead. Nor does he have a much higher opinion of Richard Tice, Zia Yusuf and the others. But even Nige has worked out that when it comes to having a Potemkin alternative cabinet, he can’t realistically do everything himself.

Only when it comes to Brexit, it seems, is Farage at his best as a one-man band. This is his battle. During Monday’s Commons statement, Andy Burnham said he didn’t want to keep “banging on about Europe”. But Nige most definitely does. Not least because the more he can talk about Brexit, the less people will criticise him for having no real plans for government. Most of his domestic policies collapse on contact with reality. As for foreign policy, he doesn’t have one. Unless you count having as little to do with the EU as possible.

The Guardian’s year in review 2026. items.title: Let’s hear it for the leftwing echo chamber | Zoe Williams

By chance, I found myself committed to a debate with people whose views I share. It was an eye-opening experience

I was on a panel recently in a church – St Luke’s in Battersea, south London – about the future of the welfare state, except the other panellists booked to speak on the right of politics were unwell and couldn’t come. And so we ended up with an entirely leftwing panel (albeit different shades of the left).

Puckishly, I suggested that I would split my six minutes of allocated speaking time and do three on what the rightwing panellists would have said, had they appeared, and then three on why they are wrong. But I couldn’t get the arguments right. I know they think the current welfare bill is – between our ageing population, our Neets and our dated expectations about what a decent life looks like and whose job it is to ensure you have one – “unsustainable”. I just couldn’t summon the right mix of tough-minded realism and benign resignation to other people’s misery. It wouldn’t come out of my mouth.

The lawsuit filed by Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Joy Campbell challenges a 2025 ICE directive that authorizes agents to conduct civil arrests in or near state courthouses without judicial warrants, which she says violates the PROTECT Act, a new state law passed ​by the Democratic-led legislature that prohibits civil immigration arrests in state courthouses without judicial warrants. The courthouse protections took effect Nov. 3.

Campbell said the ICE directive interferes with the state's authority to operate its judicial system, disrupts court proceedings, undermines constitutional principles and public safety and spreads fear, chaos and confusion.

"The Massachusetts PROTECT Act makes it illegal for ICE to conduct civil arrests in our courthouses without a judicial warrant. ICE’s intentional violation of state law has created unnecessary fear, made it more difficult to operate our courts and hold defendants accountable," Campbell said in a statement.

items.title: Talk of scrapping Natural England smacks of a government not joining the dots
items.summary:
Environmentalists say abolishing independent body will make it easier for landowners and developers ‘to trash nature’

Not just any quango, Natural England is the only public body that exists to legally protect the jewels in the crown of English nature – places increasingly under threat in a country that is overseeing an ongoing and devastating decline in its natural world.

Ecologists who work for Natural England are independent, and have the legal duty to scrutinise political decisions and ensure that short-term gallops for growth are not allowed to bulldoze forever rare and declining habitats.

Continue reading...
items.t: Abolishing Natural England would be travesty, say campaigners

items.title: Theresa May’s blast from the past calls Tories back to their unhappy place | Peter Walker
items.summary:
Conservatives may instinctively want to push back against closer EU ties, but they have to train their focus elsewhere

Anyone who accidentally switched to BBC One at about 9.45am on Sunday to be greeted by Theresa May awkwardly espousing the virtues of Brexit could have been forgiven for thinking they had woken up in around 2018 – and not being especially pleased at the idea.

This is one of the problems now facing May’s party. For all that it is a reflex action for Conservatives to push back against closer ties with the EU, Andy Burnham’s decision to pursue such a course plunges them back into their own unhappy place.

items.title: Misty-eyed Burnham gambles on closer ties with EU as he throws down gauntlet to Tories and Reform

Several sentences into a slightly convoluted answer about where UK-EU relations might go next, Andy Burnham abruptly changed tack. “The important point is that the Britain of today and the EU of today is not the one of 2016,” he said. “Life has moved on in so many ways.”

This is undoubtedly true. But Burnham’s political gamble on closer ties with Brussels hinges on the assumption that most British voters feel this way as well.

items.title: If Democrats want to win, blue-collar populists are the key | Dustin Guastella and Jared Abbott
items.summary:
Our analysis shows that ‘Bernie-Dog’ candidates are the most underrated success stories in US politics

Democrats had a huge night on 3 November. The party ran an average of about 15 points ahead of Kamala Harris’s 2024 margins, and picked up seats that Trump carried by double digits just two years ago.

Of course, the size and scope of the blue wave make it hard to draw specific lessons, and the results will inevitably serve as a Rorschach test reflecting each commentator’s prior beliefs. Democrats of all stripes won elections in all sorts of unlikely places.
